speakeroldname: Mr. Joe Clark (Leader of the Opposition):
subsubtopic: GUIDELINES FOR MINISTERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed, I suppose, to the Acting Prime Minister, pro tern, who I think is the minister of everything across the way. My question relates to an answer given by the Prime Minister yesterday to my colleague, the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton, who was inquiring about any guidelines that might exist in relation to the role of deputy ministers who serve on Crown corporations.
The Prime Minister indicated that the purpose of the presence of the deputy ministers or other representatives of the government on Crown corporations was to ensure that they represent the interests of the government. What is of concern is the possibility that their presence may confer some special advantage upon a Crown corporation; that is a matter which is of concern both to the public and to the public service. In light of the possibility of some special advantage being conferred upon Crown corporations which is not available to their competitors, because of the presence of deputy ministers, 1 wonder if the government is now considering the preparation of any guidelines to cover the conduct of deputy ministers in that kind of situation? If the government is considering such a prepara-

tion, could we have an undertaking now that these guidelines will be presented to the House of Commons?

speakeroldname: Hon. Otto E. Lang (Acting Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Minister of Transport; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
subsubtopic: GUIDELINES FOR MINISTERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, of course, it is the nature of some Crown corporations that they are in a very special position in the economy as instruments of government policy in order that certain things can be accomplished which would not happen otherwise in the private sector through the ordinary operations of the free enterprise system. In that sense, a very close relationship, obviously, is a rather natural thing.
It has been our broad practice to distinguish between those corporations which are in that position, where they are relying very heavily on ongoing votes of money from this House for their continuing work, from those others where they have a greater amount of independence and are more in the straightforward competitive field. I am thinking now of the moves we have made in relation to CN and Air Canada.
Generally speaking, I would say that as we see a Crown corporation move into the second category, we tend to move away to independent boards of directors as well and sever that closer connection except through the appropriate forms of capital budget approvals and such estimates as may be required in this House for specific projects which they undertake at our request.

subsubtopic: GUIDELINES FOR MINISTERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I take it, then, that there are no formal guidelines and, indeed, that the informal guidelines, if they exist at all, are very general. If that is incorrect the minister might want to correct it when he rises.
My specific question now is, is it the practice of the government, in relation to a Crown corporation such as Petro-Canada, to restrict in any way the activities of any deputy minister who might be present on the board of that Crown corporation to a role that would narrowly ensure that the specific purposes of the Government of Canada are accomplished by this Crown corporation? If so, is that restriction conveyed by way of any guidelines or any kind of communication?.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Minister of Transport; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
subsubtopic: GUIDELINES FOR MINISTERS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the question is essentially too general in its nature. The reason for not having a specific or single set of guidelines is that each of those Crown corporations may be quite different from the others in the exact purpose they are to serve, and in the exact relationship between the Crown corporation and the government. Therefore, if the hon. Leader of the Opposition has a specific question about a specific relationship, it would be better directed to the minister with the responsibility for the Crown corporation, or at least to the minister whose deputy minister is serving on that board.

subsubtopic: GUIDELINES FOR MINISTERS
speechtext:

areas of the economy. I am interested in the general policy that applies in this situation.

industry. As in the case of many other matters, this question must be raised from time to time.

speakeroldname: Hon. E. F. Whelan (Minister of Agriculture):
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR INCREASE IN SUPPORT PRICE OF MILK
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the formula that is used for pricing and triggering the support price for industrial milk products showed that it should be triggered, I believe, around October 1. The statistics we use are from Statistics Canada. It takes about three months to have them finalized, so that you can tell when the price should be triggered.
However, the Canadian Dairy Commission has authority to recommend to the Minister of Agriculture certain changes at any time they see fit. They recommend that at the present time we not go ahead with a price increase because it would not necessarily be beneficial to the producers of the product, as consumer buying would probably back off if the product were priced too high. In turn, they would stockpile more industrial products. We have a surplus, although not a big one, at the present time. Therefore, they would not be enjoying the extra income some think they would be receiving.
We have a new program advertising industrial dairy products which is just getting off the ground. We are satisfied that this will be beneficial. I understand the Canadian Dairy Commission will be making a written recommendation to me within the next few days on just what action we should take.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 have a question for the Solicitor General which relates to the rather

November 22, 1978

ridiculous affidavit filed by the minister under section 41(2) of the Federal Court Act denying access by Douglas Creighton and Peter Worthington of the Toronto Sun to 548 documents which reputable counsel says are necessary to their defence against charges under the Official Secrets Act.
Since this government action and that of the minister is in violation of ordinary principles of criminal law and could lead to a possible miscarriage of justice, and since it also indicates vindictiveness and bad faith on the part of the government on this particular issue, will the Solicitor General review his decision and withdraw his affidavit?

subsubtopic: ACCESS TO GOVERNMENT DOCUMENTS BY PERSONS CHARGED UNDER OFFICIAL SECRETS ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. gentleman knows full well that the charge was laid under the Official Secrets Act, and no comment is to be made by me on a matter which is sub judice. I wish the hon. gentleman would abide by the same principle.

One related to section 41(1) of the Federal Court Act and dealt with some 16,500 documents which are made available to the court in order that the court may determine the validity of the grounds I have advanced in terms of the documents themselves, in terms of their sensitivity and in terms of the necessity of not producing those documents during the trial.
As for the 548 other documents which are the subject of the second affidavit, Mr. Speaker, the reason for that affidavit being filed is simply that it relates to documents obtained from third country agencies and the hon. gentleman knows, or ought to know, that the security we maintain with third country agencies must be respected and is dependent upon the confidentiality of information received.

subsubtopic: ADMITTANCE TO CANADA OF VIETNAMESE REFUGEES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I doubt that anyone who is familiar with the plight of these individuals would deny the fact that they are refugees. It has been determined in a prima facie way by the United Nations High Commissioner that they are refugees. This is an escape route which has been found by some people.

has accepted in excess of 35,000 people who have been considered to be legitimate refugees. The Malaysian government does not want to do anything to encourage this particular trade.

subtopic: PROCEDURE IN DEALING WITH ORDER PAPER QUESTIONS REQUIRING ORAL ANSWERS
PROCEDURE IN DEALING WITH ORDER PAPER QUESTIONS REQUIRING ORAL ANSWERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 rise on a point of order with respect to starred questions and their status in parliament. I first brought this topic up in February, 1975. At that time I inquired about a question which had not been answered for approximately a month. Your answer on this point, sir, was that there was no way which you knew of by which you could enforce an answer on the particular question.
I would like to go over the history of the starred question and to say that I am fighting this case because of your position, sir, as well as the position in which it puts every member in this House, no matter on which side they sit. The starred question goes back to the time when the nation of Canada was formed. At that time the rules and regulations came from the Mother of Parliaments at Westminster.
During the Confederation Parliament of 1867 questions were put only on the order paper, and there were no oral questions or starred questions. It was not until members began to get fractious, as they do here occasionally, and were asking questions, that Sir Wilfrid Laurier, the only pure blooded French prime minister that we have had, in 1910 brought in the policy of putting an asterisk behind the question on the order paper instead of asking oral questions, because they were becoming too obstructive. The rule he introduced was that an

November 22, 1978

asterisk would be put beside the question on any given day, and the following day that question would be answered.
It was not until the years 1929 to 1955 that starred questions were no longer put on the order paper. It was the Liberal government under Mr. St. Laurent that saw the wisdom of the starred question and had the procedures committee meet, which you and I have asked for several times, to try to establish the status of the starred question as one of the important procedures of our parliamentary system. At that time one of the speakers ruled that a starred question had to be answered.
As you know, custom dictates what this parliament does over the years. There is an idea prevalent among the newer members of this House, however, that a starred question need not be answered by a minister and may be left to fade away. I think Your Honour will agree that far too many questions are left on the order paper today.
In 1955, in order to speed things up, the Liberal government under Mr. St. Laurent saw fit to establish the status of the starred question. When I came here in 1957 it was a very well known fact that a question was to be answered within a period of seven days or less. Otherwise the minister of whom the question was asked was to get in touch with the member and ask for more time. I understood that to be a courtesy, that the question might be deferred for an answer, but we see it happening every day now. A question requiring a little more research was starred for the minister. In the United Kingdom they have two days, but under Sir Wilfrid Laurier we had one day.
It all goes back to the efficiency of parliament. Some members recently elected may find it difficult to catch Your Honour's eye or even to get up and ask a question, so it is much simpler for them to put it in written form. Sir Wilfrid Laurier stated that one of the reasons for doing this was to give a member the opportunity to bring up something of particular concern to his riding but not necessarily to the Dominion of Canada. This is as relevant today as it was in his day.
One meeting of the Standing Committee on Procedure and Organization has been called in the last five years, Mr. Speaker. It was an organizational meeting and is referred to by the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert), the vice chairman of the committee, at page 4204 of Hansard, as follows:
I want to put on record that the committee has not met once during this past session except for the formal organizational meeting. Not only in this session but in the long prior session, the government House leader has refused consistently to refer one item of House rules to that committee.
I went to the government House leader about this on three occasions. The first time he told me it would probably take six weeks, and the next time he said it would take a couple of weeks. I went to him again and he said he would call it within a week because there were other things that had to go on. I know, and you know, Mr. Speaker, and all members of the
Point of Order-Mr. Rynard
House know that they do not always carry out the things they want to and, indeed, it is sometimes impossible for them to do so. But it is three times-and you're out!
Be that as it may, Your Honour also asked for help from hon. members. It puts you in a very embarrassing position not to know how to rule on a particular question. It also takes something away from parliament that two prime ministers, Liberal leaders, had seen fit to introduce. For these reasons we have tried to get the matter back before the House. I would bring to Your Honour's attention that it was not until 1964 that even the oral question was accepted under the rules.
Custom dictates why these things are done. Just two weeks ago I spoke to the President of Privy Council (Mr. Mac-Eachen), who was very courteous and told me that he would see a meeting was called to look into this, as he was not aware of the situation. Today he sent me a note saying it was unfortunate he would have to leave the House because he was meeting Mr. Vance, the Secretary of State for the United States.
That is the situation to date, Mr. Speaker. Someone is certainly dragging his feet when a member of this House does not have the privilege of asking for a ruling and for that committee to meet. I say they should all be fired, although I do not know how the House leader can be fired. I have sat in this House a good many years and found him to be a man of wisdom, knowledge, and capability. I have a lot of respect for him and I hope he will-I am sure he will-see that the committee meets.
I am not fighting this thing for myself, Mr. Speaker, but I am going to keep on until something is done, out of respect for Your Honour. I realize your decisions must be made quickly, with wisdom, with honour and knowledge, and in all conscience.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the remarks made by the hon. member for Simcoe North (Mr. Rynard) with respect to the past look fairly accurate to me. He was quite right in his description of the historical context of the rules of this House which included provisions for starred questions, and the only reservation I might have has to do with his description of my very distinguished predecessor, Sir Wilfrid Laurier who once sat as the hon. member for Drummond-Arthabaska in this House; I agree with the hon. member that he was a very great man and the terms I would use is that he was and still is a very great Canadian, a genuine Canadian, and I think it is good to point that out and refrain from making distinctions based on one's mother tongue.
With respect to the starred questions itself, Mr. Speaker, if Sir Wilfrid Laurier was right in 1910 in introducing it in the rules, things have changed entirely today. As the hon. member pointed out, he now has the opportunity to put a question during a 40-minute period every day, and if it is not urgent he can have it put on the order paper. I do not see what difference

November 22, 1978
Point of Order-Mr. Rynard
it makes whether the question he puts on the order paper is answered orally or just printed in Hansard the next day as in any case he is not entitled to a supplementary question. So the reasons which historically justified the introduction of starred questions are no longer valid today. If the hon. member has a question to ask, all he has to do is rise any day of the week and put his question to the appropriate minister. If the question is not all that urgent, he can have it put on the order paper and he will get an answer printed in Hansard. I do not see what the hon. member would gain if I were to rise and, instead of quite simply having the answer printed in Hansard, read to him an answer which he cannot debate and on which he cannot ask a supplementary question. So I think that Standing Order 39(2) could be referred to the Standing Committee on Procedure and Organization; I personally think that it is the most insignificant rule in our parliamentary procedures. And as to referring such a limited and unimportant matter in my mind to the Committee on Procedure and Organization, it seems to me that if we are to make this parliament work more effectively, as the hon. member would wish us to do, all the rules of this House should be referred to that committee. What the hon. member is actually proposing, Mr. Speaker-I mentioned this to the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) who was complaining about motions introduced under Standing Order 43 last year-represents 1/116 of our problem. There are 116 standing orders making up the rules of this House. I think they should all be reviewed together so we could modernize our procedures and make parliament younger, more modern and more efficient. And in that context I agree with the hon. member that this will provide an opportunity to review Standing Order 39(2) which I find has become insignificant in the context of 1978. But beyond that, referring to that committee only scraps of the procedures of this House I say is a waste of time, we have been procrastinating for too long and time has come to proceed with an in-depth reform which will enhance the role of members of parliament and make our presence in this House more rational, more efficient and all that to the benefit of the people of Canada.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when we concluded our sitting last night I had just reviewed a number of discursive measures of short duration employed by the government over the past 15 years to stimulate research and development in Canada. I concluded that it is no wonder the private sector has not confidence in the government's programs to promote research and development. Research programs by their very nature are long-term operations. While the rewards are great, the waiting time for results is frequently not short. The transfer of technology from government and university research laboratories to the private sector of our economy has not been accomplished with the efficiency and frequency that I would like to see.
Recent Canadian research has shown that the use of particular semi-conductors of electrodes in photoelectro-chemical batteries may be a promising alternative to the costly power lines presently used.
Basic research led to the development of soft contact lenses with enormous commercial potential. Scientists have found that a placenta derived substance may confer considerable protection against cancer of the breast.
Engineers have invented a device which enables a rapid and complete separation of the components of sugar cane. This could lead to a relatively low cost alcohol which can be distilled and used as a gas supplement. Many of these could be the invention of the decade. They are just a few of the recent
November 22, 1978

Canadian innovations which, if properly used, promoted and marketed, would assist our economy.
The government has before it a proposal from my own province, New Brunswick, that was alluded to at the recent federal-provincial conference of ministers responsible for science, research and development. The New Brunswick proposal relates to the basic resource of the province of New Brunswick, that is to say, forestry. The Minister of State for Science and Technology (Mr. Buchanan) made an announcement in this House last June about centres of excellence. He gave indications that the federal government would assist in the development of regional centres of excellence, both to build upon the diverse strength of Canada and to ensure local expertise and initiative.
The Canadian forestry service and Agriculture Canada are well represented in New Brunswick. The New Brunswick department of natural resources, the maritime forest rangers school, and the Fredericton area conservation school are also located in the area and are related to the forest industry. The University of New Brunswick has an excellent forestry faculty, and related faculties of engineering and science. It has ongoing programs such as forest extension, a fire science centre, and forest engineering. It is establishing new activities, such as a forest materials institute, a forest soils research centre, and a remote sensing research centre. The University of New Brunswick also has the largest wood lot of any university in Canada. With forestry as a principal dynamic in the Canadian and New Brunswick economies it is only right that these facilities should exist and be fully utilized.
Clearly a forestry complex which could focus the attention of all levels of government and the most advanced research on the problems of the forest industry, and transfer new technology quickly and efficiently to industry, would be a tremendous step forward in New Brunswick. I support this concept and this program strongly.
I believe that if the centres of excellence program is to have a maximum impact, it should focus its attention on programs like this and on areas that suffer from chronic regional disparity, rather than fragmenting its effort over a large area with less regional impact. I sincerely hope that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) will use his good office to encourage recognition of the forestry complex at the University of New Brunswick as one of the important dynamics in moving our economy forward.
I would ask the minister also to take another look at the $5,000 tax credit my leader mentioned in his address, for investment in small business, and to re-examine our proposal to negotiate long-term tax contracts with companies locating in slower growth areas. Both these measures are predicated on new enterprises coming into being. There is no real net loss to our public revenues by simply deferring their tax paying potential for a few years to bring them into being.
I would also ask the minister to examine the success rate of the small business program which is promoted by DREE. My impression is that this is a very good program. My deepest regret is that this discrimination which this particular depart-
The Budget-Mr. Howie
ment of government practises against Fredericton is now about to be perpetrated on the county of Sunbury which has a very high unemployment rate.
It seems that a part of the Fredericton industrial park, the new section in fact, is located in Sunbury county, and qualifies for this program, while the rest of the park does not. I am advised of a movement to disqualify all of the park. I think that the minister will find the Sunbury portion of this park is easily identified and should continue to be included in the program that is intended for Sunbury county. This is the right thing to do, and I want to bring it to the minister's attention. Indeed, I recommend that the program apply equally throughout all of New Brunswick.
Finally, I want to point to the extreme importance of enabling the universities to produce the young scientists who are essential if we are to stimulate our economic recovery through research, development and innovation, and to get back in the world markets and to get our country moving forward again. We have a double plus with the research that we promote at the university campuses. We not only improve instruction and the level of learning, but we develop excellent young scientists for the future. The $60 million or so in research and development cutbacks announced in September that are reflected in different departments of government will have to be examined on their own merits as the estimates come before our appropriate committees.
It would be premature to make any judgment at this time, but it must be embarrassing for the Minister of State for Science and Technology to announce measures to strengthen and encourage research and development in Canada, and to meet with his provincial counterparts and still not be able to produce guidelines for a procurement policy by his own government, a policy designed to encourage the purchase of Canadian manufactured goods with a high research and development component. It must be embarrassing for him not to be able to tell the minister from New Brunswick where that province's proposals for a forestry complex stand. It must be embarrassing to have to indicate repeatedly that these programs are held up in Treasury Board. But the most embarrassing thing of all must be to see the sun set on the highly visionary but rapidly fading national research and development goal of 1.5 per cent of gross domestic product by 1983. In relation to all the other industrial nations of the western world, it was a small target, but it was a goal.
The new national priority for research and development in Canada is unclear. The government is continuing its ad hoc approach to financial decision making in Canada. We have a short-term budget. There are some good measures in it, but there continues to be no long-term planning, no national industrial strategy and some good opportunities have been missed.
In concluding, I wish to refer to a telegram I received today from one of my constituents identifying a problem with the budget proposal to reduce the federal sales tax from 12 per

cent to 9 per cent. It contains a suggested remedy. I will read it and credit the author, Mr. John Clark, of Fredericton. I quote:
With reference to the recent budget whereby the federal sales tax was reduced from 12 per cent to 9 per cent it is imperative that this reduction include present vehicle inventory of auto and truck dealers. Assuming the average cost of $7,000 resulting in a tax reduction of $200 and that the average dealer has 100 vehicles in stock which is minimal then the 3,000 dealers who are members of a federation of automobile dealer associations of Canada (F.A.D.A.) would incur a loss of $60 million or more.
There is precedent for this kind of relief. In 1958 the removal of the excise tax from cars included inventory and in 1974 we received tax rebates on heavy duty vehicles.
Would appreciate any steps you can take to have 3 per cent tax reduction applicable to present dealers' inventory.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it gives me a great deal of pleasure to take part in this debate. As a Prince Edward Islander I appreciate the positive steps the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) has taken toward the preservation and expansion of industry and business in Atlantic Canada. The greatest need in that region is for a strong industrial base that will provide year-round employment and lessen our dependence on grants and subsidies from the federal government. The importance of programs like Canada Works and unemployment insurance to the Atlantic is well known to all hon. members.
No one would be happier than maritimers and Newfoundlanders to lessen the importance of these programs to our economy. The sad fact is that few large employers have found it profitable to locate outside the already prosperous areas of Canada.
There was a time when the maritimes were the economic centre of Canada. In my own province of Prince Edward Island, we at one time had a thriving shipbuilding industry. The lumber would come from our own forests, and the boats would be sailed by our own fishermen. We were self-sufficient to a far greater extent in food. One of the legacies of becoming more and more dependent on the central government was a general decline in self-sufficiency.
Maritimers are a proud people. It is not easy to accept assistance from what we call the "have provinces" when the desire is to be self-reliant and productive. It is difficult to watch each new generation leave to find work in Toronto, Calgary or Vancouver, when we know we have the natural resources, the manpower, and what should be an ideal location for carrying on trade that should make the maritimes a centre of commercial and industrial activity.
I see now a new era beginning very soon, however. There are very positive and concrete reasons for this. As I mentioned, the incentives for increased investment and research and development included in this budget should prove a tremendous boost to the economy of Atlantic Canada by encouraging the establishment of permanent industries which will continue to expand and provide year-round employment opportunities.

The budget also contains provisions for an increase from 30 per cent to 100 per cent in the write-off for development in the mining industry. This, coupled with the extension of the incentive for oil and gas exploration, should go a long way toward ameliorating our energy supply problem. There is an abundance of coal in Cape Breton, and positive signs of the existence of significant offshore oil and gas deposits. These factors provide a further encouragement for industrial growth.
The development of the region is dependent on a secure source of energy. Atlantic Canada has that energy. In addition to coal and oil, possibilities exist for massive hydro development at the Bay of Fundy and Gull Island. As well, a system of inter-connected power lines, such as that recently laid between New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island, will provide further security of supply.
The oldest industry in the Atlantic region has again become the most promising for the future I believe our fisheries are on the threshold of an era of fantastic growth and prosperity. The main reason for this change was the government's declaration of the 200-mile limit. The other reason has been the very responsible and successful policy of my colleague, the Minister of Fisheries and the Environment (Mr. LeBlanc), who has demanded that care be taken to nurture the fish stocks back to a healthy, exploitable population before beginning a program of greatly increased fishing activity.
I know the pressure the minister has been under at times to relax that policy for certain species of fish, but his wisdom has been proven by the success of his program to rebuild the Altantic fishing industry. Our main concern now will be to ensure that it is the fishermen themselves, as well as the rest of the Atlantic region, who benefit from this huge potential growth in the fisheries. This means encouraging the orderly development of a strong, independently owned fishing fleet, continued surveillance over the 200-mile limit, and programs to increase the value of the fish catch. This can be done by expanding processing facilities so that an increased amount of processing can take place in the Atlantic.
Also, there is a need for expansion and improvement of fish marketing efforts and increased exploitation of under-utilized species. I can best describe my optimism concerning the future of the fishing industry by comparing it to the discovery of oil in Alberta, only our oil is swimming in the ocean.
One development of which I am particularly proud is the move of the headquarters of the Department of Veterans Affairs to Charlottetown. This, of course, is in keeping with the government policy of decentralization, the reasons for that policy being well known. They bear repeating, however, for they demonstrate the commitment by this government to positive action to counter regional disparity. That attack on regional disparity is certainly a primary consideration in a relocation of this magnitude.
It should also be remembered that by decreasing the concentration of public servants in this part of the country, we are responding to a widespread feeling that the federal bureaucra-
November 22, 1978

cy, by being cloistered in the national capital region, is insensitive to the needs and concerns of Canadians from coast to coast. The proportion of public servants in the Ottawa area is up to twice that of federal employees in the capitals of other western nations. This policy of decentralization, therefore, has my unqualified support. It is only fair and just that Canadians in all parts of Canada-and we all pay federal taxes-should benefit as greatly as possible from the presence of the federal government throughout the land.
With particular reference to the move of DVA headquarters to Charlottetown, the benefits which will spread to all parts of the province are very significant and exciting indeed. For just the construction phase of the relocation, our studies indicate that the direct impact will be to create approximately 300 jobs. About $5 million will be paid in wages and salaries for those jobs.
During the operating phase we estimate that the number of jobs available for Islanders to compete for will be from 350 to 450. The wages paid to Veterans Affairs employees on the Island should total approximately $10 million per year. Of this it is projected that about 70 per cent, or $7 million, will be spent by those employees on various commodities every year, with most of that, presumably, being spent on the Island. The impact of this spending by DVA employees will, it is estimated, mean the creation of approximately 250 new jobs over and above those new jobs within Veterans Affairs headquarters. In addition we have estimated that the total indirect income generated will be in the area of $2.8 million.
Additional local employment and income are expected to be generated by the ongoing expenditures necessary for the operation of the departmental headquarters. It is anticipated that approximately 77 new jobs will be created, and that additional income of about $675,000 will be generated as a result of annual head office expenses of $1.8 million.
Including this indirect employment, along with the number of employees who will be working at DVA headquarters, we arrive at a total figure of around 1,000 new jobs being added to the Prince Edward Island work force. The total additional income created by the move has been estimated at about $15 million per year.
In a province with a total population of just over 120,000, an employer providing 1,000 jobs is obviously going to have a major impact, not just on the economic life of the province but also on the social and cultural areas. For a city of its size, Charlottetown already boasts considerable cultural amenities and educational facilities. The involvement of Veterans Affairs staff in the various activities of the community will be most welcome.
I see this relocation of a federal head office as one of the keystones of the economic development which is about to take place in Prince Edward Island. It is a non-polluting industry which will not have a negative impact on the high quality of life on the Island. The department will require the services of diverse professional, clerical and other support staff, thereby providing opportunities at home for our youth now enrolled in college and university. It is an incentive for our young people
The Budget-Mr. MacKay
to remain and help with the developing of our other resources. That will mean putting the emphasis on those areas in which we do our best, and ensuring that the maximum added value is placed on our products before they are exported.
Farming and fishing will remain the economic mainstays of the Prince Edward Island economy. The increasing sophistication of these industries demands the continued updating of our knowledge in those fields, and I am hopeful that the research and development incentives which have been so substantially increased in this budget will be used to full advantage to benefit those two very important areas.
Liberals have been criticized recently for being too optimistic and expressing too much confidence in the future. I feel strongly that at no time in the last few decades has there been more reason to be hopeful about the future prospects of my own province and Atlantic Canada in general. A new frontier has been opened up with the 200-mile limit, the possibilities of which are endless and not yet even dreamed of. The energy resources I mentioned earlier are real and in the process of being developed. Moreover, there is a new realization on the part of maritimers that their area, with its long history and well-known and envied spirit of community and common cause deserves another chance to regain the proud place it has held in the past. There is a quality of life in the maritimes that cannot be found anywhere else in Canada-a concern for one's fellow man, and a sense of identity which was never broken by the economic privations of the past. With the bright future ahead, those traditional values and qualities will stand us in good stead as more prosperous days become a reality.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I consider it a privilege to follow the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. MacDonald). I think he made a fine speech and I commend him for his optimism, speaking as he does as a representative of the last provincial outpost of liberalism. As we know, very shortly the present administration will have presided over the complete disintegration of federal liberalism in this country.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
