subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Well, the minister, with that indomitable Scottish fighting spirit, says "Don't fool yourselves". But 1 think he would be quite willing to concede privately that the chances of halting the onslaught of the leader of the opposition, Mr. Angus MacLean, in Prince Edward Island, are almost negligible at this point.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Another good Scot.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Yes, another good Scot. Which makes it all the more difficult to do.
Mr. Speaker, to start off this speech on a gracious note, I was interested in the very sincere tribute paid to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) by the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mrs. Holt). I thought it was a most deserved and gracious tribute, and I would like to associate myself with much of what she said.

November 22, 1978
The Budget-Mr. MacKay
The Minister of Finance, who brought down this budget, is certainly held in great esteem as a person by all members of this House. However, I must say in all candour that I think his talents do not lend themselves to the portfolio which he holds. It has been suggested that to ask the minister to adjust our economy is like asking the Boston strangler to adjust your necktie! I don't believe it is quite that bad, but I see the member from Toronto who represents small business here in the House today and perhaps he would agree with me that the minister has had about as much success in the financial league as the Argonauts have had in the CFL during the past few years.
In any event, Mr. Speaker, there are measures in the budget which do deserve some commendation. The federal sales tax reduction and the removal of the special excise tax on marine engines, private aircraft and motorcycles, were measures that were applauded by those opposite when they were imposed, and are now applauded just as vigorously when they are removed. So you see this government is capable at times of learning from its mistakes. The sector and regional incentives are also sound moves. However, the minister's room to manoeuvre in this budget has been severely limited by past mistakes, excesses, and mismanagement on a massive scale during the last number of years by this government.
Huge expenditures on non-productive projects have put our country in a position where funds for worth-while projects of the type which I am sure the Minister of Veterans Affairs would agree would be appropriate for the Atlantic region, are hard to come by. They are hard to come by because of past mismanagement and there just aren't enough funds available to go around any more.
The initiatives regarding the unemployment insurance legislation, which were proposed in the name of restraint and in an attempt to save money, are commendable. However, there are some pitfalls which I see implicit in what the government is doing. These amendments have to be fine-tuned in committee in an attempt to prevent the savings being made at the expense of people in those areas of the country where there are no jobs to be, shall we say, an object of evasion. There is really no disincentive factor which affects the maritime region at this time because, frankly, there are no jobs there, in most cases, for people to avoid taking.
A reduction in premiums is risky at this time. It is welcome in some ways, and while it is tempting to look upon premiums as a tax because they are deducted at source, they really are not. Although contributions will be $300 million less, unless unemployment insurance benefits are reduced accordingly, the savings on premiums will become increased government expenditure, and the increased spending will have to be financed either by increased revenues or higher deficits, neither of which is desirable.
I think the government should take a very hard selective look at what it is doing with respect to unemployment insurance legislation because it is not in the Atlantic region, where

the problem is greatest, that the abuses are taking place. The abuses are taking place in the more prosperous areas of the country, and they are being perpetrated by middle income families who are systematically using unemployment insurance to supplement their incomes.
A lot of money has been lost by this government through foolishly conceived projects. Certain tax concessions, however, have been made in slow growth areas. I think they are well intended, but, frankly, I had hoped to see in this budget a greater input from DREE; for example, a widening of eligibility of the industries which can participate in DREE programs to allow industries other than manufacturing and processing to benefit from DREE grants, provided they meet the other criteria. I think this would have been a sound thing to do, and I am sorry the minister did not see fit to do that in his budget.
Another thing which should be done soon-and again unfortunately it was not done in this budget-is to reduce some of the confiscatory aspects of the capital gains tax. Many sound financial people across the country have been urging the government to consider, if not abolishing the capital gains tax, at least modifying it. Our party strongly believes that it must be indexed and perhaps done away with altogether because the benefits received are not commensurate with the harm done to the free enterprise system. As has been said by a former deputy minister of finance of many years, Dr. Kenneth Eaton, it is a bad idea, that a tax on capital gains comes mainly out of capital or out of income that otherwise would be saved for capital formation. The absence of a tax on capital gains, while ordinary income is being taxed at high rates, results in a positive incentive to capital formation, particularly equity capital. On both counts, therefore, in a country which must import capital for development, a tax on capital gains is not a good idea.
I also suggest to the minister that capital gains taxes to some extent are inflationary because when people are confronted with capital gains taxes their first reaction is to ascertain how much extra they have to pay in tax, and they adjust their asking price accordingly in an attempt to get away with as much profit-deserved in many cases-as they can.
I think that the incentives given to the mining industry are acceptable, but if it came to weighing the balance of benefits it would have been more appropriate to have been a little less generous in that field and to have applied some relief on the capital gains tax side in order to provide incentives and promote the desire to take the risks which have always been part of the Canadian industrial and development psyche. To have had this present tax in place has done immeasurable harm to the development of our country.
Another thing which has been counterproductive to some extent-and I do not think it was thought through carefully enough, particularly when nothing was done about the capital gains tax-is the way that the minister singled out certain small business service corporations, which have been incorporated and have been paying taxes as small businesses, and made it impossible for them to obtain the preferential small business tax rate. This measure does not apply to small
November 22, 1978

businessmen engaged in production or trade. Although the wording is somewhat unclear, this measure seems to catch doctors, dentists, accountants, professors, management consultants, entertainers, journalists, engineers, and other professionals who have structured their financial affairs so as to qualify themselves as businesses. This kind of ad hoc measure which is being taken by the minister, while well intentioned- particularly in the absence of relief for small business on the capital gains side-is not, on balance, a good thing for the economy.
Even though by some measurements our country is nearly broke because of our excessive borrowing and spending in the past for needless capital works projects and things of that nature, about which we all know and which we have discussed many times in this House, there still has to be some massive capital works expenditures if we are to promote growth and better the standard of living in areas of Canada such as the areas which the Minister of Veterans Affairs and I represent. I come again to the merits, for example, of a corridor road through northern Maine which could, in partnership with our American friends, provide important benefits to Atlantic Canada and some to the United States. It would greatly facilitate tourism and the marketing of Atlantic Canada products. Transmission facilities to bring electricity to Prince Edward Island and Nova Scotia are critical. The minister referred to this as well.
These projects require the expenditure of vast amounts of money, and there is no choice but to proceed with them because high energy costs are hampering the standard of living and the prospective development of this important region of our country. Greater efforts must be made if this part of Canada is to realize the destiny it must achieve.
This government has had some very strange fiscal and financial policies. I want to mention specifically the situation with regard to Canada Savings Bonds. Last August in a newsletter the Bank of Canada made reference to the maturing of past issues of Canada Savings Bonds. On October 1 the 1968 special replacement series, SR, came due, followed by the 1969-70 series, S-24, on November 1. Over 900,000 Canadians held maturing bonds worth approximately $2.6 billion. In addition, said the Bank of Canada in its newsletter, accumulated interest and cash bonuses on the bonds added an additional $ 1.9 billion to the amount coming due.
My point is that on the current issue of Canada Savings Bonds, of the initial $4.5 billion, $2.6 billion will be for refunding purposes and $1.9 billion to cover the cost of accumulated interest and special bonuses.
I think that Canada Savings Bonds ought more often to be a topic of discussion and consideration in this House because having such a large percentage of our national debt in call money, whereby holders may redeem their investments at any time, has proved to be very costly. In each period of high interest rates investors have rolled their issues into better rate bonds, or the government has reacted, as it has done again-it had to-by raising the interest rates on all outstanding issues. Substantial fees are paid to advertisers and to financial institu-
The Budget-Mr. MacKay
tions. In addition, there are many hidden charges tied to the Bank of Canada internal process. I believe that Canada Savings Bonds should be available through the payroll system and to small investors. The government should periodically announce the rate of interest which is payable and adjust the rate up or down to reflect current conditions.
There are many financial problems facing this country, but one of the reforms which should be implemented is a change in government policy regarding our debt financing. After all, when we are faced with a deficit of $11 billion or $12 billion, which works out to about $1 billion a month over the year, it is shocking that we must meet our interest obligations by borrowing. I trust that the Minister of Finance will look into this and make the needed adjustments.
I see my friend the Solicitor General (Mr. Blais) is in the House today. I would like to say a few things about the McDonald commission of inquiry in the context of the budget debate. I think it is quite relevant to do so because it is financed through the Privy Council office, the budget expenses of which have increased about 78 per cent over the past few months.
I think that the McDonald commission is something in which many members of parliament and most people in Canada are very interested. They hold great hopes for its success. I have a few comments to make which are constructive suggestions. I hope they will be of some use, and I hope they will be accepted in the spirit they are given. I am under the impression that the maximum information available is not coming out in the hearings to date. Also, I have some concern that the talents of all counsel are not being utilized to the fullest. In some areas I have the fear that counsel are not asking the right questions, and perhaps from the investigative side some potentially valuable witnesses are not being contacted.
I should like to deal with two main areas of interest to the commission. They are mail openings and the relationship of the security service to the Department of National Revenue. When a case file or files are opened on an individual by the security service, always there are two parallel files, one of which is secret. When an investigating officer decides that they merit hard investigation, a number of procedures are available. There are telephone taps, surveillance, checking tax records, mail openings such as Operation Cathedral, and so on. But practically all these procedures must be approved by the officer in charge of the division, and then sent to headquarters in Ottawa for final approval. As the Solicitor General well knows, periodically warrants are brought in for his personal signature.
Let me first speak of mail opening. My impression is that the commission and the Canadian public need to know a great deal more about the scope, size, and the procedure of this operation. For example, in almost every sizeable city in this nation an interface has existed for many years between the security service and the Post Office. The "watcher" service of

November 22, 1978
The Budget-Mr. MacKay
the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, which many people do not know about, also was an important part of the operation outside the Post Office. In Ottawa, if it has not already done so, the commission might consider contacting Mr. Harry Hurd, who has had major responsibilities in this now civilian oriented service. As a matter of interest, it takes a lot of personnel to keep a suspect or target under 24-hour surveillance. For two suspects at a time, on a 24-hour basis, perhaps as many as 200 people are required.
Let me come back to the procedures involved in opening mail. I know the Solicitor General is interested, because who could ever forget the expression on his face that day in the House as Postmaster General, when his colleague, the then solicitor general, told him, yes, in fact mail was being opened? I will speak in the past tense because I do not know exactly what is happening today. When a person was being followed and posted a letter, a large envelope about the size of the interior of the post box immediately was dropped in by the person observing him. All of the mail below that envelope, which sealed off the box, was then available to be opened.
One could say, "How did they get access to the post box?" It is very simple. The superintendent of a shift of the "watcher" service had a key. The mail was opened in due course and examined In many cases it was opened on a wholesale basis. By necessity it involved a lot of people who had nothing whatsoever to do with the target or suspect, but' whose mail just happened to be below that strategically inserted envelope. So much for mail outside of the Post Office.
When one looks at local post office one finds some other very perceptive and definite methods of operation which were followed. For example, in Montreal Sergeant Rick Neal happens to be the contact. I am sure the commission would want to talk to a man like Rick Neal. His job was to check with the designated supervisor or person at the Post Office and collect mail periodically which was set aside for that purpose on a daily basis. He brought the mail to the identification laboratory where it was opened and, if appropriate, photographed and processed. Sometimes it was brought back to the post office in the same day, which at least is very commendable. I emphasize that this type of operation does not exist in merely one or two isolated instances. It is nation-wide. It must be approved by the appropriate security service officer in the division. In Montreal it would be someone like Chief Superintendent Cobb or one of his predecessors, Chief Superintendent Larry Forrest or Ray Parent. At any rate, it has been going on for years.
Before an "Operation Cathedral" is put in place, as I said, each one has to be approved by RCMP headquarters and by the Solicitor General, in theory. This is from where the commission ought to seek additional information, by asking officers in charge across the country just how long this situation has gone on. My information is that this has been going on for many years. Indeed, I spoke with an officer who told of setting up photographic facilities in a post office in an out-of-the-way spot in an attempt to develop techniques which would allow mail to be photographed without being opened.

All of these things are relevant, because I am convinced that sufficient testimony has not been brought to the attention of the public or the commission, about the scope of the operation. Goodness knows there are many witnesses whom I suggest the commission might want to contact. Perhaps they have contacted some of them, but I do know the commission has not seen fit to bring Warren Hart back yet. He opened mail on a wholesale basis in Toronto. They should talk to Don Cobb, or perhaps the director of the security and investigation services branch of the Post Office in Ottawa, Mr. Paul Boisvert.
As the Solicitor General would say, "without breaching national security", let us have a look at what the RCMP security service has been doing in offices of the Department of National Revenue across the country. I am not talking about the CIB branch or the correspondence which was exchanged between the then solicitor general and the then minister of national revenue. This correspondence has been alluded to in the commission hearings. I am talking about contacts over the years between the RCMP security service and the Department of National Revenue. There were everyday methods by which the security service would be in touch with its contact men in the Department of National Revenue. The security service would then be handed a complete file on one of its targets. I do not believe that type of procedure could be justified, unless there was ministerial and departmental knowledge involved.
I commend to the commission for questioning, for example, Superintendent Fernand Bosse, if they have not questioned him already. Superintendent Bosse of "C" Division in Montreal would go into the National Revenue office and talk with his contact there. I understand at one time his contact was a man in the verification and collection branch of Taxation Canada, Mr. Cote. He would say to Mr. Cote, "I want a file". It could be the file on anyone. Mr. Cote would bring him the file, and he would look at it. If the file was informative, then he would have complete access to it. But, as I understand it, if the file was not sufficiently or completely informative, he would say to his contact at National Revenue, "Go and do an investigation", and an investigation or audit would be done.
I do not want to belabour this point. I do not want to drop names and hurt people who are doing security jobs in the national interest. I do not pretend that I know it all, or even very much, but I am disturbed about what I have learned so far. The counsel and investigators are more to be faulted than the commission itself, because they have not asked the right people the right questions. The Solicitor General would be well advised to talk to more rank and file officers in the security service, assuming indeed he wants to talk to them. It is no secret. This has been going on for years and years. Practically anyone of any rank in the security service knows about this. The reason they are not testifying about it is that they are not being asked the correct specific questions. In some cases counsel are so ill-informed or have done so little homework that they do not know the type of questions to ask, and the answers complicate matters even more.
I will make the Solicitor General an offer. If he wants to, on a confidential basis I can tell him of a man who will go before
November 22, 1978

the McDonald commission and testify in great and specific detail about a lot of things which so far have not come out.
1 got the impression from ex-Commissioner Higgitt's testimony that "Cathedral" operations were fairly seldom invoked procedures about which he knew nothing, or very little. If Commissioner Simmonds had said that, it would have been more credible because he did not spend very much time, if any, in security services. Ex-Commissioner Higgitt spent almost all his time in security services. I would put to the Solicitor General and to the commission, through you, sir, that surely in the national interest, since this commission has been given such an important mandate, it should take a more in depth approach to what it is doing and should contact people such as some of those I have mentioned here today.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not know how many budget debates in the course of the last seven or eight years I have taken part in, but I am not particularly pleased to participate in this one. However, I feel an obligation to the House, and particularly to my constituents, to enter into this debate, not entirely in a negative way, but certainly to bring attention to and to counter some of the statements made in a general sense by Liberal speakers, and to bring out the meat or lack thereof in the budget, as this will affect the average Canadian, those lower and middle income people who pay most of the taxes in this country and contribute most in terms of numbers because they make up the largest group.
The message delivered in the budget is clear. The government and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) have abandoned any pretense of providing economic leadership in this country. At a time when unemployment is high, when inflation is running at close to 9 per cent and real growth is lagging far behind expectations, what we need is a dynamic program of economic recovery. What we got was a do-nothing budget that will not even inject enough stimulus into the economy to undo the damage done by the government's spending cuts announced during August and early September.
In this budget the government has deliberately chosen a policy of slow growth and high unemployment, in short, a policy of economic stagnation. The victims, as always, will be the unemployed, and the average Canadians who are trying to cope with inflation.
Apparently the reason for the finance minister's budgetary inaction is his belief that the economy will perform as well in 1979 as it did this year, although 1978 was hardly an impressive year in terms of our economic performance. There is no indication in the minister's budgetary remarks, as there has been from private economists, that the economy is likely to weaken next year in line with a U.S. recession. Rather, the government is trusting the United States to ensure our continued economic stability. The budget makes the unsupported assumption that the United States will achieve real growth of 3 per cent this year, despite the fact that American forecasters are predicting hard times in that country that could cut growth to 1 per cent at best. We cannot wait for the Americans to bail
The Budget-Mr. Blackburn
us out. They are just as much in trouble as are we. It is time to embark on a course of forthright and independent economic action. One look at the finance minister's forecasts for 1979 will underline this fact.
We know now that Canada will not achieve 5 per cent growth for this year as the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) pledged at the Bonn economic summit. He said we would achieve 5 per cent this year, but obviously we will not. In fact our growth this year is likely to be closer to 3.5 per cent and, according to the Minister of Finance, growth will not increase much next year either, when the best we can hope for is 4 per cent or 4.5 per cent. This is significantly lower than the 5 per cent rate of growth required just to hold unemployment at present levels. The minister recognized this when he forecast only 250,000 jobs will be created in 1979. That is 110,000 fewer jobs than were created in 1978 which has been a year of record unemployment.
In light of the fact that this budget will increase the number of Canadians without jobs it is understandable the minister neglected to mention in his remarks that unemployment is likely to climb to 9 per cent next year. Prices, according to the minister, would increase 6.5 per cent. This is higher than earlier recovery path projections made by the finance department, but still lower than this year's 8 per cent or 9 per cent increase. Unfortunately the minister gives very little justification for his inflation estimate beyond his oft expressed hope that there will soon be a dramatic turn around in food prices. If there is a significant drop in inflation it will certainly not be as a result of his efforts in this budget.
As one listened to the Minister of Finance and other members on the government side who spoke during this debate, one got the impression that he was still listening to R. B. Bennett and Herbert Hoover. We are back in the 1930s when prosperity "is just around the corner."
Given these forecasts, Canadians can be forgiven for believing the government would introduce budgetary measures designed to improve our economic performance. This is especially true considering that the majority of economic forecasters have indicated that growth in 1979 will be substantially lower than the minister's own projections, and that inflation will be substantially higher.
I have before me seven economic outlooks for 1979, issued by various banks, securities firms, and advisory bodies, all of which suggest the minister's figures over-state the health of our economy. The most optimistic of the private forecasts was issued by the Conference Board in Canada, and puts growth at
3.7	per cent, inflation at 7.4 per cent, and unemployment at 9 per cent. The most pessimistic of this group of references was issued by Wood Gundy, which puts growth at 2.2 per cent, inflation at 7.6 per cent, and unemployment at 9.1 per cent.
Faced with these discouraging economic forecasts, the minister had a clear responsibility to stimulate the economy. As he said at page 5 of the budget, and I quote from his statement:
Consumer spending rose by less than was expected, and this was the main reason for the shortfall in growth.

November 22, 1978
The Budget-Mr. Blackburn
This opinion has been seconded by economic experts who have pointed to the fact that the minister's last two budgets failed precisely because they did not provide enough stimulus to boost the purchasing power of Canadians. Without more purchasing power in the economy, business simply cannot afford to expand and jobs will not be created.
The budget before us today demonstrates that the minister has not learned from his mistakes. He ignored the advice of his government's own economic advisory body, the Economic Council of Canada, and, I might add, of my own party, the NDP, and refused to make personal income tax cuts of any real significance.
We have to inject money into the economy in order to put people back to work. We in our party have estimated that a $1.5 billion tax cut, through increasing purchasing power and the accelerated economic activity it would promote, would create up to about 100,000 new jobs.
Certainly the Minister of Finance tried to show in his remarks that he was injecting stimulus into the economy but, despite the impressive snow job, the fact remains that he did not. This becomes painfully clear when we examine the specific provisions of this neutral and ineffective budget.
The only real tax cut in the budget is the doubling of the maximum employment expense deduction from $250 to $500 annually in 1979. The government estimates this will put $270 million into the economy and that 6.2 per cent of the 11 million taxpayers in this country will benefit from the change.
However, because Canadians will still be required to claim for only 3 per cent of their income up to the $500 maximum, those Canadians earning less than $8,333 a year will not receive any benefit from this cut, and those earning over $16,666 a year will get the full benefit, that is, up to $500. Once again, in typical Liberal fashion, the rich get richer and the poor get poorer.
It is time that the government tried to revitalize their very antiquated tax policies. The effect of the increased employment expense deduction to the average taxpayer earning $12,000 a year, will be $110 a year more in deductions. If he is taxed at a rate of 20 per cent, he will receive a tax cut of between $20 to $25 a year, or about 50 cents a week. The story is much the same for the unemployment insurance premium cut highly touted by the minister, where the rate will decrease from $1.50 to $1.35 per $100 of insurable earnings for employees and, from $2.10 to $1.89 for employers. This means that Canadians will be taking home approximately 35 cents more a week, or about $18 a year. I am basing my calculations on the maximum insurable earnings allowed under the UI plan, which will be $11,700 in 1979.
There are a lot of people in this country who make far less than $11,700 a year, and they will not even get 35 cents off their payments a week. It will be less. However, it should be noted that while premiums are being reduced, unemployment benefits are being drastically cut back as part of this government's restraint program, from 66% per cent of insurable

earnings to 60 per cent. This is very significant, not only for those who are getting the maximum UI benefits, but also for those who are getting minimum benefits.
It is not generosity which inspires this premium reduction, since the Unemployment Insurance Act legally requires that contributions be cut when the unemployment insurance fund is running at a surplus. This is currently the case, so the minister had no choice. Yet he made it look as if he was giving this paltry 35 cents a week out of the goodness of his heart.
Together the increased employment expense reduction and the UI premium cut add up to less than $1 a week for the average Canadian. This is hardly enough to boost significantly consumer spending in this country. In fact, it is nowhere near enough to help the average family even catch up to inflation, which I would remind hon. members, by all the best forecasts for next year, will be at least 9 per cent if not higher.
Although the minister attempted to make next year's 9 per cent indexing increase in personal exemptions sound like a new tax exemption, Canadians are not so easily fooled. This exemption results from the automatic adjustment of tax rates to past inflation, and was introduced by this House into the Income Tax Act in 1974. In fact, it is a means to prevent the government from automatically raising taxes due to inflation, and not in any way a tax cut that can be spent by the consumer.
The cut in manufacturers' sales tax from 12 to 9 per cent is the most positive aspect of this budget. It is a proposal which we advocated and which we welcome. However, by itself it is not enough. The federal sales tax cut will continue the stimulative effects provided by the retail sales tax cut contained in last April's budget, but it will be far less effective. First of all, the cut amounts to only $1 billion over the whole of 1979, whereas the retail sales tax cut amounted to more than $1 billion over a six to nine month period. In fact, the economy will suffer net loss in stimulation.
Secondly, and more significantly, there is no assurance the cut will be passed on to consumers. The finance minister states that "experience suggests that such tax cuts are passed on", but he knows that is simply not the case. What generally happens is that much of the impact is lost among the middlemen. The minister's appointment of three government agencies to monitor the cuts shows he is aware of this fact. This is true whenever you take away part or all of a hidden tax; immediately prices tend to drop, and then there is a mysterious tendency for those prices to climb slowly back up again within six months, and this is not necessarily due to inflation.
Although this cut goes into effect immediately, its impact will not be felt until current inventories are run down. The best that can be hoped for, if the benefits are passed along to consumers, is a reduction of one-half of one percentage point in the cost price index next year. To this extent the measure is at least a step, albeit a tentative one, in the right direction.
Disregarding for a moment an analysis of the altogether more generous incentives provided for business in this budget, the government says the total impact of its measures will be a
November 22, 1978

$1.38 billion cut in taxes in 1979. This level of stimulation is far short of the $2 billion worth of spending cuts that have been taken out of the economy in recent months.
When the Prime Minister returned from Bonn last August with his pledge to stimulate the economy toward 5 per cent growth, he said this would be accomplished "by reduction in both our expenditures and our taxes". We have seen the spending cuts, but we are still waiting for the tax cuts. The government, in its policies announced last August, and in this unbelievably regressive budget delivered last week, is actually restricting the economy.
For the one million Canadians who want to work but cannot find a job, this hold-the-line budget offers no hope. Without stimulation in the economy, unemployment is likely to climb over 9 per cent, not go down. Canada is in a mess now as far as unemployment is concerned, and here the government is bringing in a budget that will not only not stimulate the economy, but will exacerbate the unemployment problem and make it even worse.
The minister has given generous incentives to business and the resource section to expand, but even if jobs are created- and experience suggests they often are not-these will take at least a year to materialize.
The unemployed need jobs now, and what was needed in this budget was an immediate program of public investment in transportation, housing and public works projects. My party has long been advocating such a program, which would put an estimated 225,000 people back to work. Spending on needed facilities in communities where they are lacking is infinitely preferable to the make-work programs the government has relied on in the past few years. For example, we need a $400 million federal-provincial-municipal capital works program. This has been demanded by the premiers of the provinces and supported by most municipalities. Such a program would create 60,000 new jobs.
The second element in our program is a $500 million investment in modernizing and rebuilding Canada's obsolete rail system. This would provide better grain transportation facilities and has been recommended by the Hall commission. It would create 70,000 jobs.
Thirdly, we have suggested a $300 million urban transit program which would improve much needed rapid transit services in major cities. This project has the recommendation of the Prime Minister himself, who committed the government to just such a program on the eve of the 1974 election. Or perhaps the Prime Minister has forgotten. At any rate, we believe this would create 40,000 new jobs. I suggest that the Prime Minister remember that proposition, particularly in the city of Toronto, considering what happened in the by-elections there.
Finally, we need a $500 million special housing program which would provide funds for non-profit, co-operative and public housing, and also for neighbourhood improvements and residential rehabilitation projects. These are socially oriented programs on which the government could spend money that
The Budget-Mr. Blackburn
would in turn go to the purchase of goods and services and thereby get the economy moving again. This need is particularly acute in view of the fact that the housing market and construction industry are seriously depressed, and that high interest rates and land prices make it impossible for many Canadians even to consider buying their own homes. The minister's only housing proposal in the budget-a tax shelter for land speculators and developers-certainly will not improve this situation. We estimate our program will create
70,000	jobs in the construction industry.
Unfortunately, rather than having the courage to introduce innovative programs, the government chose to stand pat. That is precisely the reason for the economic malaise in this country. The government refuses to take the positive economic action required to reduce unemployment, to stimulate growth, or to chart a course toward economic recovery.
Even more glaring than the government's failure to come up with immediate, short-term measures to deal with our economic problems is the minister's failure to plan for the future. Other countries plan for the future, but this government seems to be very sluggish about it. There is no strategy in this budget. In fact, in his budget remarks the minister said, as reported at page 1199 of Hansard'.
I am frankly skeptical about the search for a single grand industrial strategy in a competitive market system.
I do not believe that there is just one basic strategy for the next five years, seven years or four years or whatever, but why does the minister at least not bring in a budget that would give us several alternatives so that we could plan ahead for our monetary and fiscal activities? The Minister of Finance refuses to recognize that government has a vital role to play in the economic management of our country. Canada does not have an industrial strategy, and until we have another government, we probably never will.
1 think the minister has been listening to too much conservative talk across the country. After all, private enterprise plans years ahead, whether in the manufacturing or resource oriented industry. I cannot, therefore, understand why Conservatives say that private enterprise should plan ahead, but that they do not have to and can operate on an ad hoc basis and blunder their way through. Even more glaring than the government's failure to come up with immediate short-term measures to deal with our economic problems is the minister's failure to plan for the future. As I said, there is no strategy in this budget. I quoted the minister as saying that he is frankly skeptical about a search for a single program.
The aim of such a strategy would be to develop the industries involved in the key sectors of our economy, such as housing, transportation and food. Instead, the government scatters its development incentives all over the place, without knowing the consequences. That is why from the same government we get budget incentives to increase research and development in this country, but drastic spending cuts in the research budgets for fisheries, farming, forestry and transpor-

November 22, 1978
The Budget-Mr. Blackburn
tation. This budget will grant at least $750 million to businesses through new tax cuts and the extension of existing ones. These will supplement the billions of dollars provided to corporations in previous budgets.
The government should seriously examine the consequence of its policy of across-the-board corporate tax cuts. I will not dwell on any specific examples here, but it is relevant to note the effect such cuts have had on a corporation such as Northern Telecom. Going back a few years I will use two examples of tax concessions, rapid write-offs and concessions that previous ministers of finance have used as vehicles to stimulate the economy but which did not stimulate the economy.
Northern Telecom has received close to $14 million in federal grants and loans. As of December 1977, its deferred taxes were about $50 million. In addition, the Export Development Corporation has loaned $200 million to foreign countries to buy Northern Telecom equipment. Between 1971 and 1977 sales doubled and profits increased from $12 million to $85 million. Yet while the company profited from the government's "no strings attached assistance," Canadian workers and the Canadian economy have been less fortunate. In the early 1970s, Northern Telecom employed 26,000 people. Last year, it employed 15,000 and by the end of 1978, 1,000 more jobs are expected to be lost. Obviously the government's program of corporate incentives is not working. It is certainly not working in the interests of the employees or of consumer demand.
Inco is another well known beneficiary of the government's corporate largesse. Between 1967 and 1976 Inco had a profit of $1.7 billion, and could defer $368 million in taxes. It also received $17 million in tax credits and a low interest $70 million loan from the Export Development Corporation to develop operations in Indonesia. The result was 3,000 people laid off in Sudbury and Thompson last year.
These abuses, Mr. Speaker, are precisely why we need an over-all industrial strategy. Instead of across the board tax cuts for corporations, which only increase the deficit and do nothing to decrease unemployment, the government must take an active hand in directing where its investment in business goes and what it will be used for. Instead of handouts with every budget, the government should be prepared to negotiate long-term planning arrangements with the corporate sector.
In other words, there should be strings attached; taxpayers' money should not be just handed over to the government to create a certain number of jobs within a certain period of time. Of course, once that obligation was fulfilled, the lay-offs would begin with the excuse that there was something wrong with the market or with the product. Industry could always find excuses to lay people off and cut back on the cost of operation. Specific tax incentives should only be granted to specific corporations in return for the company's pledge to do more research and development or increase investment in Canada.
For this reason, I question some of the incentives included in what can only be described as this "pro-business" budget. The government is extending the investment tax credit for an indefinite period and raising it from 5 per cent to 7 per cent. Is such an incentive really necessary when the government tells

us plant utilization has already increased from a low of 82 per cent last year to 87 per cent now?
This credit has not worked in the past as an incentive for companies to expand and create new jobs. All too often, the money has simply been used to re-equip plants with more up-to-date equipment, with the result that fewer employees than before are needed to produce the same amount of goods. With plants already expanding, there is no justification for the continuation of this credit.
I would like to reiterate once again, Mr. Speaker, that if the government is going to grant incentives out of the public purse, those benefits must be directed to create jobs, to promote research, and to benefit the economy. Across the board incentives to companies do not and will not accomplish the purpose for which they were intended.
We need more planning, and this will mean more government direction of our economy. That will require more courage than this government demonstrated in its budget, where it has managed once again to avoid its responsibility to put people back to work and get Canada growing again.
A few moments ago I alluded to the impression I have that the Prime Minister, the Minister of Finance and other members of cabinet are listening to conservative elements in the country with the feeling that perhaps there is a great wave of conservatism moving from one ocean to the other. I dispute this. The results of the by-elections, and particularly the result of the provincial election in Saskatchewan a few days afterwards, show that although people may be conservative on certain specific issues, certainly in my riding in southwestern Ontario and in other parts of the country people are not taking a broad, general, small "c" conservative attitude to every aspect of government and every aspect of life. We still have progressive thinking people in the country and we still have great numbers of reform-minded people. I think it is a shame that in a panic, knowing he has only a few more months to go, the Prime Minister is prepared to bow, to bend, to twist and to cater not just to moderate "c" conservative opinion in the country, put to large "C" Conservative opinion, politicized, of course, in the Progressive Conservative party.
The Prime Minister would do well to be his own man for the next two months. Instead of giving in to pressures from my colleagues to the extreme right, he should think things out for himself and remember the purpose of small "1" liberalism as well as the philosophies of social democracy-philosophies which he espoused ten years ago. As a result of certain pressures being brought to bear on him by certain outspoken and vocal conservative elements in the country, he seems to have forgotten those philosophies and be prepared to go the conservative route in order to get votes.
I notice my time is just about up, Mr. Speaker, but I should like to say that people in this country are demanding action. They did not get action from this budget. They will not get action and they will not get assistance. Business, particularly small business, the main street retailers, shopkeepers or whatever term one wishes to use, will not benefit either. What businesses need is customers. They do not need government
November 22, 1978

assistance and hand-outs, they need customers, and if they do not have customers they are in trouble. Businesses will not have more customers as a result of this budget. This budget will not in any effective way increase the purchasing power of ordinary Canadians who make up the vast majority of the consumers in Canada.
I do not know how many times we on this side of the House, particularly we in the NDP, have to drive the point home to the Liberal government that people need money. They need substantial tax breaks in order to increase their ability to consume. In this way we can get things moving again and not have to sit back with a constrictive budget waiting for Uncle Sam south of the border to bail us out. In the interests of the Canadian public I hope that over the next few months the government will pull itself together, get some new blood in it and attempt to rectify and turn around what is at the present time a depressing economic outlook.
