speakeroldname: Mr. Pierre Bussieres (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Science and Technology
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the night of the budget, I was both astonished by and happy about the attitude of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien). I was astonished because everybody knew what temptations the minister had to fight against in the preparation of his budget in the present circumstances, and I am not thinking only about the fact that there is a general election coming, but also about the fact that various groups had given him pieces of advice as to what to include in the budget.
The Minister of Finance, and I am quite pleased, has proceeded in a responsible manner, in a prudent manner that the previous speaker has identified as being a certain conservatism, but prudence is not conservatism; respect for reality and prudence about decisions which are extremely important for the future of the country and all Canadians is not a conservative but a responsible attitude.
Mr. Speaker, it was strange to hear some commentators on budget night say that there was nothing in the budget, that there was no substantial personal tax reduction and so on. Mr. Speaker, such an attitude was all the more ironic that, had there been substantial personal tax reductions in the budget, we knew that the same commentators would have said that the Minister of Finance was an opportunist looking for vote-catching manoeuvres before the general election, but as they could not lay that charge, they said that there was nothing in it. Mr. Speaker, it is obviously extremely difficult to please everyone and when a politician adopts a responsible attitude it is seldom recognized. That responsible attitude on the part of the Minister of Finance is obvious in the main objectives of the budget. The first objective is to allow our industry to maintain and increase its capacity to be a serious competitor in international markets. That, Mr. Speaker, is extremely important for us Canadians.
The Budget-Mr. Bussieres
Its second objective, Mr. Speaker, is to keep inflationary pressures as low as possible. Obviously it would be tempting to resort to the solution proposed by the New Democratic Party and to slash personal income taxes thus increasing purchasing power but one had to ask himself seriously, and that is what the Minister of Finance did, what effects such cuts, that extra flow of money would have on inflationary pressures; whether such a decision might not precipitate a new wave of inflation, and whether it might not reach the level we have known in the last few years but have now managed to contain. The danger was that much greater that we are just coming out of a period during which controls were applied to subdue inflationary forces. I am happy that the Minister of Finance resisted that suggestion and took a far more responsible decision, namely that of containing inflationary forces by refraining from opening too wide the gates of purchasing power.
Mr. Speaker, we also know that those forces could have led to greater expectations in salary demands destroying what we managed to get from all workers, that is recognition that lower increases were needed as compared with those we saw during periods of development. They recognized themselves that it constituted an inflationary force; as we know, a renewal of high demands in salary increases would exceed the present capacity of the Canadian economy.
As I see it the fourth objective is designed to stimulate investment in as many Canadian firms as possible. I shall refer later on, Mr. Speaker, to some measures which can actually help us achieve this new economic impetus. Finally another objective has to do with research and development in all sectors of the Canadian industry.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to speak about some measures that will enable us to achieve these objectives. First, the reduction of the federal sales tax from 12 per cent to 9 per cent. I think this measure is very significant and that everybody should be involved not only the manufacturers but also those who are situated between the Canadian manufacturer and the Canadian consumer to see that this reduction is actually passed on to the consumer. If we can achieve these objectives, I am sure that everybody from the producer to the retailer will recognize the useful repercussions of this measure on the economy and that they will help the government reach these objectives by passing on this 3 per cent reduction to the Canadian consumer, for not only will the consumer benefit from this but also the business firm because reducing the price of goods by 3 per cent will create the demand, which had been the purpose of previous tax cuts, by lowering the cost to the consumer by 3 per cent. I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that this measure is of significant importance.
Mr. Speaker, I reiterate my trust in all intermediaries between the producer and the consumer. I dare hope they will do their utmost to pass this reduction on consumer goods on to all consumers.

November 22, 1978
The Budget-Mr. Bussieres
There is a second point which I want to emphasize, Mr. Speaker, in connection with personal income tax. For instance, with fiscal year 1979, the deduction for employment expenses will be increased from $250 to a maximum $500. It will enable 6.2 million taxpayers in Canada to take advantage of a tax deduction representing a loss of revenue of about $270 million for the government. It is extremely important.
Someone said earlier that with a reduction in personal income tax it would be possible to put more money in the consumer's pockets; well, those $270 million will in fact go into the pockets of the Canadian taxpayer to enable him to buy more new goods. This is a relief from employment expenses.
The third measure, Mr. Speaker, relates to the indexing mechanism which is incorporated in the Income Tax Act. We know that it was already implemented and that it will reduce federal tax by $1.2 billion next year. I come back once again to what was said earlier about the request for sizeable tax cuts, and 1 shall say that this indexing provision makes it possible indeed to put new funds in the hands of taxpayers.
Mr. Speaker, there is also a provision about registered retirement savings plans which will benefit minor or disabled children where their parents die. Furthermore, Mr. Speaker, the budget provision concerning unemployment insurance will benefit the employer or the employee. It will also enable us to stimulate our industry.
Mr. Speaker, now I would like to say a few words on provisions which will affect more particularly our economy in terms of natural resources. Among those provisions, I want to mention first the investment tax credit. This provision, as everybody is aware of, is extended for an indefinite period and above all its rate is higher. Also, although not limited to natural resources it will benefit that sector significantly because of its regional impact. Indeed the rate is raised to 20 per cent in the Gaspe area. Recently I was listening to the hon. member for Gaspe (Mr. Cyr) commenting on what is happening in Murdochville and Madeleine mines and I am sure he is very happy that this increase to 20 per cent should apply to his riding.
I am also convinced that all hon. members from the Atlantic provinces share the opinion of the hon. member for Gaspe. In the other designated areas it was increased to 10 per cent. These include the major part of Quebec, all northern Ontario and western Canada, except for the southern part of Alberta and British Columbia. Since most future investments in mining and forestry will be in these areas, the impact of this measure is far from being negligible for the mining industry. Thus most of the $500 million allocated in the first year by the recently introduced budget will affect the sector of resources in the areas I have enumerated.
Exploration and development in the mining and oil industries will be particularly encouraged by the new measures

reducing considerably the corporate tax paid by companies operating in this sector. For example, new mining development expenditures will be deductible at 100 per cent instead of the 30 per cent rate previously used. That is a considerable raise, Mr. Speaker. That is to start from 30 per cent and say that from now on everything you spend to develop new mines will be deductible. Expenditures incurred by resource industries for new social assets or local facilities will be eligible for the additional deduction of $1 for every $3 spent, as will the expenditures for exploration and development of the industry itself. This would increase the interest on investments and stimulate the economy of many mining areas. This measure would also improve the welfare of the people living in those areas where mining facilities are being installed.
The Department of Finance has estimated at about $25 million the cost to the federal government of these two measures.
The accelerated amortization of pollution control equipment is extended indefinitely. We all know, Mr. Speaker, that it is extremely costly to instal pollution control equipment, either in the energy, mining or paper sectors, and companies engaging in such programs will be granted a tax reimbursement. This will also be in the interest of the people living in those areas, as we are increasingly conscious of the dangers of pollution for those people. As the mining industry is going through a period of uncertainty, this extension will be very beneficial to them. It is sometimes difficult for companies which are experiencing overproduction and a reduced rate of profitability to make the necessary expenses in the fight against pollution in order to improve the quality of life. That measure will help us in the pursuit of our objectives relating to the quality of the environment, and at the same time it will stimulate the economy in many regions.
The extension of incentives for drilling funds is also an extremely positive measure. That program, which was supposed to expire on June 30, 1979, gives individuals an opportunity to get directly involved in oil and gas research through a drilling fund and to benefit from the generous incentives offered to that industry. That program also makes it possible for us to find right here in Canada the capital needed for the implementation of our energy policy. The extension of that measure will only confirm our commitment to government policy and our determination to take all necessary steps for its implementation.
There are other things, Mr. Speaker, and I quote:
Extension of coverage to transportation
The coverage of the investment tax credit is to be expanded to include expenditures on rail, air, water and ... road transportation equipment. The basic rate of credit of 7 per cent will apply to all such qualified expenditures.
Mr. Speaker, we know that many and substantial investments are necessary in the transport industry, and you will see that this measure will be particularly helpful to the mining
November 22, 1978

industry transporting, for example, sulphur, potassium and coal.
I would now like to say a few words, Mr. Speaker, about the business transaction that allows all Canadians to be able to say that today their oil company, Petro-Canada, is now one of the giants in the oil industry. By acquiring Pacific Petroleums, Petro-Canada has become one of those giants. As a Canadian, Mr. Speaker, I am very proud of that transaction and I suspect that most Canadians are going to reject the idea of the Leader of the Opposition who would sell the Canadian corporation that is Petro-Canada.
I would like to point out what I believe to be a great abuse of language, namely that that was an act of nationalization. I do not believe, Mr. Speaker, that it can be said that that transaction freezes government funds and requires serious outlays by the government at a time of spending restraint. As was suggested on several occasions in this House, the purchase by Petro-Canada is a business transaction in which all the rules of business transactions were followed. Petro-Canada went and got its funds through the Canadian banking system and bought shares of Pacific Petroleums. So that transaction is a business deal, and Petro-Canada through the profits it will derive from that new organization will be able to invest a lot more in the research for and supply of energy in Canada. That will allow us to achieve the objective of meeting more than 70 per cent of Canada's needs in petroleum products. That purchase will also allow us to have better guarantees as to our reserves of energy. The amounts generated by Petro-Canada will also allow us to reduce the government expenditures that will be necessary to give Petro-Canada a second breath, new energy and a new financial capacity to broaden its operations.
And, as was said and repeated, Mr. Speaker, that purchase was made without having to use government funds but on a commercial basis, financed through the banking system.
Mr. Speaker, those were the few remarks I wanted to make on the budget and I am sure all Canadians will give their support to those budget measures, they will also give their support to that transaction, and 1 would invite them to read the editorial in today's Toronto Star which contains an excellent analysis of the attitude of the Leader of the Opposition with respect to the purchase of Pacific Petroleums by Petro-Canada.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 should like to preface my comments, if I may, with a special word of appreciation and thanks to all my workers in the recent by-election in Ottawa Centre for their efforts, for the long hours they put in and, in many cases, for the sore feet they suffered, indeed for everything they did in responding so well to a hotly contested campaign. I am highly indebted to them for their efforts in getting me into this House. 1 should also like to take the opportunity to thank the electors in
The Budget-Mr. de Cotret
Ottawa Centre for the clear-cut mandate they gave me to represent them in this place. Finally, 1 should like to thank all the hon. members in this House who have helped me make the transition to parliamentary life as easy as it has been in the last month.
It is with great pride and very real humility, Mr. Speaker, that I came forth one month ago to this chamber to represent the people of Ottawa Centre. It is a responsibility I do not take lightly, particularly at this time in our country's history. The challenges are great and the opportunities before us unparalleled in the industrial world. Yet as 1 travelled across this land I could only detect to my sorrow a lack of confidence in our ability to meet these challenges, uncertainty about our future and, indeed, fear at our current situation.
These deep-rooted concerns among Canadians are graphically portrayed by the comments and queries of my constituents in Ottawa Centre. To many to the east and to the west of us, Ottawa Centre appears as a constituency unique in Canada. It is a riding situated at the heart of the nation's capital. Its topography is graced by rivers, lakes, canals and parks. It is the riding in which this House is located and as such it is the major focal point of political activity in this country.
Yet in reality, Mr. Speaker, far from being highly unique and highly favoured, the riding of Ottawa Centre is in most respects a microcosm of Canadian society. The income level of my constituents parallels very closely that of Canadians as a whole, ranging from wealth to poverty. So does the educational background of my constituents parallel that found elsewhere in Canada. While there are many employed in the service industries, not the least important of which is the federal government, Ottawa Centre also has a strong constituency of small businessmen, of professionals, of tradesmen, of construction workers.

Mr. Speaker, the constituency of Ottawa Centre also has ethnic characteristics which are comparable to the ethnic diversity of our country. Moreover, there are as many tenants as homeowners in Ottawa Centre. This constituency is therefore very representative of Canada as a whole in many respects.

But, Mr. Speaker, Ottawa Centre is not a highly favoured riding. It is a riding which suffers a rate of inflation equal to, or higher than, that of most major urban centres in this country. It is a riding which, surprising though it may be to people from elsewhere, unfortunately has a rate of unemployment which is generally higher than the average for Canada as a whole. In this respect the concerns and expectations of the people of Ottawa Centre mirror well those of many Canadians. In electing me to the House last October 16, the people of Ottawa Centre gave me a strong mandate to speak out, and speak out strongly, on their behalf and to make their concerns known in this forum of public debate.

November 22, 1978
The Budget-Mr. de Cotret
In addition to these general concerns, there are also considerations over and above the over-all situation of the economy of this country, of the state of the nation as a whole and of the management of the public sector. My constituents are concerned about the industrial future of Ottawa Centre in the near term; and they are concerned about the relocation program of the federal government and the policies the federal government intends of pursue unilaterally in terms of its employees.
But, Mr. Speaker, today-
[ Translation]
I would especially like to talk about the proposals made last week by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien), concerning the present economic situation in Canada as he sees it. I would therefore like to talk briefly about the economic situation in Canada. However, I am getting more and more concerned, Mr. Speaker, to find so many different opinions and different interpretations about the present economic situation. I also deplore the fact that the debates often become personal attacks. To underline my concern, Mr. Speaker, I would like to mention as an example, the recent discussions in public forums such as this institution about the situation on the labour market. If we talk about unemployment during such debates, we are quickly accused of being prophets of doom. However, if we look only at job creation in Canada in the last 12 months, we always forget to talk about the unfortunate situation of those who attempted to join the labour market without success. I have another example, Mr. Speaker.

Another example, Mr. Speaker, of this divergence in the interpretation of current economic conditions, can be found in the debate over the rate of real output growth in this country. Less than a year ago I had, I believe, the unique distinction of being in full agreement with the Minister of Finance in terms of the prospects for the Canadian economy in 1978. Both our evaluations of possible developments this year, led us to believe that real output would grow by 5 per cent. Yet, Mr. Speaker, for the government that 5 per cent, became a goal to be achieved and against which it has fallen short, while for us it was a barely acceptable economic performance that desperately needed to be surpassed through more aggressive economic policies.
Other examples of widely diverging interpretations of the same numbers abound. I need not detail them because I feel I have made my point. Essentially, my point is that the current situation hardly provides an environment of factual analysis, that leads to appropriate policy proposals.
What, then, is the current economic situation against which the measures introduced last week by the Minister of Finance must be evaluated? First let me talk about the positive elements, because there are many. Let me start by calling attention to our human resources.


First of all, Canada is a young nation with a young, dynamic and aggressive manpower. If we compare the age of Canadian workers on the basis of the total Canadian population with the average age of the population of our main trading partners, we find that Canada's population is much younger on the average. The Canadian population also has an education level greatly superior to that of the manpower of our trading partners. If we look first of all at access to education, we find that in Canada, between ages 3 and 34, 49.8 per cent of the population enjoy direct access to the educational system, which is much more than the percentages of 44 per cent in the United States, 22 per cent in the United Kingdom, 16 per cent in West Germany and 23 per cent in Japan.
If we look at another statistic, Mr. Speaker, which concerns the number of years spent full-time in the educational system in Canada, between ages 7 and 25, we find that Canada ranks third among the countries of the OECD, behind Sweden and the United States. In addition to a young, aggressive and well-educated manpower, Canada has an abundance of workers, which instead of being described as one of our great advantages, is often thought to be one of the weaknesses of our system and one of the main causes of our high unemployment. For my part, I like to consider this abundance of workers as one of the positive factors of the seventies and future decades. [English]
The human resources of this country are unparalleled in the industrial world. They are the cornerstone of the future development of this country, particularly as we enter the 1980s. To the same extent that our human resources are the cornerstone of that development, our physical resources are the tool of that development.
Let me assure this House that we are far from being deficient in physical resources. Let me name but a few. We have a total forestry inventory equal to that of the United States. We have proven oil reserves per capita twice those of the United States. Proven gas reserves per capita are two and a half times larger than those found in the United States. In terms of cultivated land we have a factor of 2Vi per cent per capita over the United States. Our uranium resources per capita are three times the size of those in the United States. I need not tell the House that we exceed by much larger factors the wealth and resources of countries such as the U.K., West Germany and Japan.
Turning to our mining sector, our production levels for nickel, zinc, copper, potash, asbestos, uranium and iron ore, to name but a few, surpass absolutely those of our major industrial trading partners. If they do not surpass in absolute terms, they do in terms of per capita production.
Our resources are not running out. We have an abundance of resources left in the soil. That is our potential, and realizing that potential will be the main challenge facing Canadians in the 1980s.
November 22, 1978



But to date, Mr. Speaker, our economic performance remains far short of the potential I have just indicated. I would like to take a few moments to deal with the economic conditions now prevailing in Canada. At this point in time, in the last months of 1978, we find ourselves in a period of economic stagnation that has been going on since the 1974-75 recession which, it will be remembered, is the most severe experienced since World War II. Since that time our economic performance record, although it may be considered acceptable based on certain international comparisons, is indeed noticeable for its failures to realize our potential. We have been performing much below our potential. In 1975, our growth rate in real terms was 1.3 per cent. In 1976, thanks to a strong first quarter, growth was 5.5 per cent. In 1977, the figure was 2.7 per cent and to date, this year, we have had a first quarter where real growth was 0.7 per cent, and a second quarter where growth was only 1.1 per cent.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, over that 13-quarter period, ever since the 1974-75 recession, we had ten quarters when economic growth in Canada was below the level needed to accommodate the increase in the labour force and to maintain the level of our industrial capacity utilization. In other words during three quarters only of those three years did we experience the kind of economic growth this country needs to fulfil its potential.

If we consider current economic indicators, about which we hear in this House every day and about which we read in the newspapers of this nation every day, there is very little to lead one to make a statement as to the emerging recovery of this economy. Our real domestic product is increasing at a rate of approximately 2'h per cent per year. Our industrial production is increasing at a rate of less than 4 per cent per year. When we consider new orders, retail trade, machinery and equipment, we find indicators which show no great vigour and no move toward a sustained recovery.
In terms of housing starts there has been a very serious slump over the last 12 to 18 months. Only when we look at employment creation do we find a glimmer of hope. That will soon be dashed by labour force growth, the increase in the number of those Canadians who are legitimately entering the labour market to seek employment. There again by comparison there is a significant shortfall, and there will be a consequent increase in the rate of unemployment.
I have described our economic potential and our economic performance to date. There is a very great distinction between our potential and our actual economic performance. The fact that there is a difference between our potential and our performance is the tragedy of this government. This government has been unable to understand and appreciate, in policy terms, the distinction between what we can be and what we are at the moment. I can say only that no amount of comparisons with countries which are not as well endowed with natural
The Budget-Mr. de Cotret
resources as we are and which are not as fortunate as we are in terms of human resources will hide from Canadians the basic fact that we are experiencing some very serious economic difficulties.
We must not compare our economic performance with that of other industrial countries, because at this time and into the 1980s we are and will be a country which stands in a class of its own, given those resources and our potential. The meaningful comparison which has to enter public debate and serve as a basis for policy formulation is that between our actual performance and the potential we know we can realize. In that respect I am afraid we will find ourselves seriously lacking in terms of initiatives. We will find ourselves in great need of new policy directions, new initiatives, new leadership and, in one word, new government.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
In response to the current economic situation and to our potential, let me review briefly what the policy stance in this country has been and how it has evolved in the last 12 months. Let me say very boldly that 12 months ago we had a more aggressive and a more expansionary monetary policy. Twelve months ago we had a more aggressive and a more expansionary fiscal policy. Over the last three years, the monetary targets set forth by the Bank of Canada, as a prime indicator of its policy direction, gradually have been reduced from a range of between 8 per cent and 12 per cent to a range of between 7 per cent and 11 per cent last year; to a range of between 6 per cent and 10 per cent this year. The last reduction to a range of between 6 per cent and 10 per cent was accompanied by no less than six increases in the bank rate, leading to unprecedented high levels of interest rates across the country.
That is not to say that is a restrictive policy. Money is available, but money is very expensive. It is a high priced policy. But definitely it is a policy which is less expansionary than that which we could find in the country only 12 months ago.
On the fiscal side, the situation is much the same. We have gone from a position where we had temporary income tax cuts earlier this year to a temporary reduction in sales taxes. Recently we have seen the end of that measure, the introduction of significant expenditure cutbacks, and in this latest set of proposals from the government the reintroduction of only a small part of the stimulus which we could find in the economy in the earlier months of this year.
When I look at the measures presented by the Minister of Finance in his budget last Thursday, I find the biggest criticism which can be directed toward those measures is the one which flows logically from my comments-that we are not addressing the question of our economic potential.
There are specific measures in the budget which must be applauded. Let me applaud them and name them. I was happy to see the government make a move, as timid as it may be, in

November 22, 1978
The Budget-Mr. de Cotret
the area of manufacturers' sales tax. Also I was very happy to see the investment tax credit measures introduced. I think the R and D initiatives are in the right direction; we have been talking about that for a long time. The move in the area of resource taxation is one which should be applauded, as well as the employment expense deduction. This is something we have favoured and recommended to the government over the past several months.
When one looks at the over-all budget, what does the government offer to Canadians? Certainly it offers no hope that Canada will enter in the near future a period of economic recovery and sustained economic growth. It offers another year of 4 per cent growth, a rate of growth which is inferior to what is required to accommodate new entrants into the labour force. It offers employment creation of 250,000 jobs, which is exactly the same number as the increase in the labour force, if we assume absolutely no increase in the participation rate. I know the minister would be the last person to make a forecast of the participation rate, or for that matter the unemployment rate. In my own timid way, let me say that given the social and economic environment in this country, I expect to see continued increases in the participation rate. On that basis, a job creation forecast of 250,000 inevitably leads to a forecast of higher unemployment for the 12 to 14 months to come.
With regard to inflation, the minister offers the hope to Canadians that our inflation rate next year will be about the same as it is this year. The budget does nothing to restore the stimulus we had in the system earlier in the year. The budget does nothing to offer Canadians the reasonable expectation that they will know better economic times in the next 12 to 18 months. It is a stagnation budget.
In looking at the over-all budget, my second observation is that it is a short-term budget. I am not sure if that should be viewed as a criticism, because in the tradition of recent budgets it seems to me that all we can expect is a five-month budget from the government. It is a budget of adjustments of the margin. It is a budget which does not deal with the very critical problem of addressing where we are going as a nation in the 1980s and 1990s. It is a budget which gives no indication of direction or goals, and no commitment to stability in policy. In fact, it is a budget which is a stop-gap measure. It is a stand-fast budget which inevitably will lead to the continuation of the period of economic stagnation which we are now experiencing. The proposals introduced in the guise of a budget do nothing to help Canadians realize the potential they have and to get Canadians, as they have in the past, enthusiastically behind a move toward economic prosperity.
In conclusion, I should like to address specifically three myths which have been perpetuated in the public debate generally, and to some extent in the recently introduced budget measures. The first myth I should like to dispel is that at best in Canada we can expect an economic performance equal to that of the United States. Have we forgotten that over the years we have had a stronger growth in income per capita in Canada than in the United States? Have we forgotten that in the whole post-war period we have had more rapid produc-

tivity growth in Canada than in the United States? Have we forgotten than on average over this period we have had more rapid real growth in Canada than in the United States?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Because of the Liberal government.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: We have. To suggest that the best we can achieve is a rate of real growth equal to the United States, and that we should be thankful for that, should be put aside immediately. We can and we must achieve a rate of economic development, growth and wealth generation in the country to allow the kind of distribution of income we would like to achieve. We must and can achieve a rate of economic development superior to that of the United States.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The second myth I should like to talk about briefly is that only a high level of unemployment will solve inflation. I am sure members of the House will remember that myth because it has been widely publicized across the country. Have we forgotten the costs of unemployment, the costs of having available human resources who are non-productive? There are human costs, social costs, and some very real economic costs which must be borne by the rest of us who are productively engaged.
In an environment in which there is rampant excess demand, inflation, shortage of manpower, shortage of goods and in which we are facing bottlenecks, certainly a higher level of unemployment traditionally has led to a decrease in inflationary pressures. But in an environment in which no such pressures exist from the demand side, in an environment in which there is ample excess capacity, in which demand is weak, and in which unemployment is hovering between the 8 per cent and 9 per cent level, the economic and social costs of unemployment, far from decreasing inflation, are fed right through the line, add to the over-all cost pressures on the economy, and contribute to a higher rate of inflation. At that point the policy prescription is clear: we can fight both unemployment and inflation at the same time. I remain firmly convinced that that is an objective which we should set for ourselves.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The third myth which I was most disappointed to see emerge in our nation approximately a year and a half ago is that Canadians must accept a slower rate of growth, no doubt a justification for the fact that our rate of growth already was quite slow. What exactly does that myth mean? When we look at it on a per capita basis, does it mean that we must accept permanently a higher rate of unemployment of human resources? If not, the only other thing it could mean is that we must accept permanently a lower rate of productivity growth.
Very frankly, I reject both. We need not accept a higher rate of unemployment of human resources We have all the means at our disposal to achieve at least the same kind of productivity growth in the next decade or two, as we have in the last decade or two. On a per capita basis, we can and we
November 22, 1978

must achieve the kind of economic growth this country is capable of, given its potential.
If I have been able to dispel these three myths, Mr. Speaker, what must we accept? The basic proposition is that we must accept that Canada's potential is unique among industrial nations; we must accept that this potential has to be addressed; we must accept the need for a set of comprehensive strategies and policies to ensure that Canadians can maximize that potential over the decades to come. The Progressive Conservative party in the last several months has put forth suggestions, policies and initiatives that would provide Canada with just that type of policy-not a marginal policy, not a policy of adjustment or of tinkering and not a policy to deal with specific issues, but a framework in which the potential of this nation is clearly identified and against which policies can be introduced to help maximize this potential. These are policies dealing with individuals, housing, small business, the corporate environment and labour relations. These policies have been made public and we will discuss them further.
These are the policies for the 1980s. They are the policies of hope and they are the policies of a country that will realize its potential in the next decade.
